title: INTA Updates & Maintenance Center
description: Unified update inventory, package-manager-aware application maintenance, Windows servicing, repair, uninstall and failed-update recovery.

channels.name: Windows Update
channels.scope: Operating system, cumulative updates, servicing stack, feature upgrades
channels.note: OS servicing is separate from third-party app package managers. Feature upgrades, drivers and firmware require separate checks.

channels.name: WinGet
channels.scope: Applications recognized by Windows Package Manager
channels.note: Respect package pins, source identity, unknown versions and installer scope.

channels.name: Chocolatey
channels.note: Package scripts are executable. Review source, pin, license and package scripts.

channels.name: Scoop
channels.scope: Apps installed through configured Scoop buckets
channels.note: Only Scoop-managed packages appear; review bucket trust and app persistence.

channels.name: UniGetUI
channels.note: Manager health and package operations are available through its CLI; verify supported manager and installed CLI version.

channels.name: Ninite Pro Classic
channels.note: Commercial license required. Pro Classic CLI differs from the newer Pro web interface.

channels.name: Microsoft Store
channels.note: Store updates are separate from WinGet and Windows Update.

channels.name: APT (Debian / Ubuntu)
channels.note: Use only on Debian/Ubuntu derivatives; review transaction plan.

channels.name: DNF (Fedora / RHEL)
channels.note: Use only on Fedora/RHEL-family systems; review transaction and reboot requirements.

channels.name: Pacman (Arch)
channels.note: Arch requires full system upgrades; never perform partial upgrades.

commands.title: Audit Windows Update history
commands.summary: Read recent Windows Update Client events to identify failed KBs and HRESULTs.
commands.safety: Read-only. Event availability and provider names vary by Windows build. Keep raw logs private and redact device identifiers.

commands.title: Open the supported Windows Update troubleshooter
commands.summary: Launch the Windows Update troubleshooter / Get Help flow supported by the installed Windows version.
commands.safety: Opens Settings. Follow the recommended troubleshooting steps; do not bypass managed update policy or safeguard holds.

commands.title: Inspect Windows Update services and pending reboot indicators
commands.summary: Inspect Windows Update service state, reboot-related registry indicators and free system volume space.
commands.code:
Get-Service -Name wuauserv,bits,cryptsvc,msiserver -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Format-Table Name,Status,StartType -AutoSize
Get-Volume -DriveLetter C | Select-Object DriveLetter,HealthStatus,SizeRemaining,Size
$paths = @('HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\WindowsUpdate\Auto Update\RebootRequired','HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Component Based Servicing\RebootPending')
$paths | ForEach-Object { [pscustomobject]@{Path=$_;Present=(Test-Path $_)} }
commands.safety: Read-only. Reboot markers are indicators, not authoritative proof that a restart is required. Do not alter service startup types as a generic fix.

commands.title: Reset Windows Update download caches with a reversible backup
commands.summary: Stop update services, rename SoftwareDistribution and catroot2 to timestamped backup folders, then restart services to allow Windows to rebuild caches.
commands.safety: State-changing recovery action. Use only after collecting the update error and trying the supported troubleshooter. Requires admin and a maintenance window; temporarily stops update services, causes update history/download cache to be rebuilt, and can require another download. If either rename fails, stop and inspect service state before proceeding. Do not delete the timestamped backups until Windows Update succeeds and retention is approved.

commands.title: Repair Windows servicing component store and system files
commands.summary: Use DISM to repair the component store, then SFC to validate protected Windows files when logs indicate corruption.
commands.safety: State-changing repair; allow each command to finish. Use matching installation media if DISM requests a source. Capture exit codes and logs; do not interrupt servicing.

commands.title: Open Windows Update diagnostic logs
commands.summary: Open the Windows Update operational log and generate the readable Windows Update ETL log when needed.
commands.code:
Get-WinEvent -ListLog '*WindowsUpdate*' | Select-Object LogName,IsEnabled,RecordCount
Start-Process 'eventvwr.msc'
# Optional: create a readable Windows Update log on the desktop
Get-WindowsUpdateLog -LogPath "$env:USERPROFILE\Desktop\WindowsUpdate.log"
commands.safety: Read-only diagnostics except for creating the local text log. Logs can contain system identifiers and update metadata; store privately.

commands.title: Reset Microsoft Store cache
commands.summary: Run the supported Store cache reset utility when Store downloads or updates are stuck.
commands.safety: Clears the Store cache and opens Microsoft Store. Does not uninstall apps or guarantee a repair; use only for Store-specific symptoms.

commands.title: Inspect Windows Installer service and recent MSI failures
commands.summary: Check Windows Installer service state and recent MsiInstaller events before retrying an interrupted MSI setup.
commands.code:
Get-Service -Name msiserver | Format-List Name,Status,StartType
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Application'; ProviderName='MsiInstaller'} -MaxEvents 40 | Select-Object TimeCreated,Id,LevelDisplayName,Message | Format-List
commands.safety: Read-only. Installer event logs can expose application names, paths and account context.

commands.title: Repair an installed MSI application through its registered product entry
commands.summary: Open the registered Windows Installer maintenance UI so the technician can select Repair when the vendor MSI supports it.
commands.safety: GUI-driven. Select the exact application and use Change/Repair only if the registered installer exposes that action. Do not guess product codes or run msiexec /f against an unknown package.

commands.title: Inventory installed applications before update or uninstall
commands.summary: Capture installed applications from standard uninstall registry locations without invoking deprecated Win32_Product enumeration.
commands.code:
$roots = @('HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*','HKLM:\Software\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*','HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*')
Get-ItemProperty $roots -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object DisplayName | Select-Object DisplayName,DisplayVersion,Publisher,InstallDate,UninstallString | Sort-Object DisplayName | Format-Table -AutoSize
commands.safety: Read-only. May reveal licensed software and user-installed applications. Registry entries may be stale or incomplete; do not execute an UninstallString without inspection.
commands.sourceTitle: Microsoft Windows Installer uninstall registry key

commands.title: Preview available WinGet application updates
commands.summary: List detected WinGet updates before making changes; review pins, sources and package identities.
commands.safety: Read-only inventory. WinGet cannot update every installed application and may not know versions for some packages. Check pins and package sources.

commands.title: Apply reviewed WinGet updates interactively
commands.summary: Update packages WinGet identifies as upgradable while retaining interactive installer prompts.
commands.safety: Changes installed software. Preview with `winget upgrade` first, inspect package identity, publisher, source and pins, and schedule a maintenance window. Does not cover Windows OS, Store, firmware or all vendor updaters.

commands.title: Repair one application with WinGet
commands.summary: Use WinGet's supported repair command for a single identified application when its package/installer supports repair.
commands.safety: Replace Publisher.Package with the verified exact ID from `winget list` / `winget show`. Not every package supports repair. Do not use --ignore-security-hash to bypass integrity failures.

commands.title: Uninstall one identified application with WinGet
commands.summary: Remove one application after confirming exact package identity and user data retention requirements.
commands.safety: Replace with the verified exact package ID. Uninstall may remove app data or shared components depending on the vendor installer. Back up required settings/data first; never use a guessed ID.

commands.title: Open WinGet diagnostic logs
commands.summary: Open WinGet's log folder to inspect the failed package operation.
commands.safety: Opens local logs; sanitize usernames, paths, source URLs and machine details before sharing.

commands.title: Inspect WinGet sources before resetting them
commands.summary: Check WinGet version and configured sources when searches or updates fail.
commands.safety: Read-only. Do not reset sources as the first step; managed/custom sources and policy may be intentional.

commands.title: Reset WinGet default sources
commands.summary: Restore default WinGet sources only after recording current configuration and confirming custom sources are not required.
commands.code:
winget source list
winget source reset --force
winget source update
commands.safety: Changes source configuration and may remove custom source entries. Export/document custom sources and check policy before resetting. This does not repair every App Installer issue.

commands.title: Preview Chocolatey package updates
commands.summary: Review outdated packages and preview the upgrade-all transaction without applying it.
commands.safety: Preview only. Review sources, package scripts, pins, exclusions and license/edition. Package scripts are executable code and can run with elevated privileges.

commands.title: Upgrade reviewed Chocolatey packages
commands.summary: Apply Chocolatey package upgrades after reviewing outdated list and no-op preview.
commands.safety: State-changing bulk operation. Do not bypass pins, force reinstall, ignore checks or silently assume package scripts are safe. Use a maintenance window and retain transaction logs.

commands.title: Uninstall a Chocolatey-managed package
commands.summary: List locally managed Chocolatey packages, then uninstall one exact package.
commands.safety: Replace package-id with the exact installed package ID. Package uninstall scripts may remove data or dependencies; inspect package metadata and preserve user data first.

commands.title: Clean Chocolatey package cache after confirming a cache issue
commands.summary: Inspect Chocolatey cache statistics and remove expired HTTP cache entries when a stale cache is implicated.
commands.code:
choco cache list
choco cache remove --expired
commands.safety: Chocolatey CLI 2.1.0 or later. The command removes expired cached HTTP items; it does not delete all cached packages. Cache behavior depends on elevated context and the user/system HTTP cache. Review cache stats first.

commands.title: Inspect Scoop-managed application updates
commands.summary: List outdated apps installed through Scoop.
commands.safety: Read-only. Scoop only manages packages installed from configured buckets; bucket trust and manifest scripts matter.

commands.title: Update Scoop-managed apps
commands.summary: Refresh Scoop and update Scoop-managed applications.
commands.safety: Changes user-managed software. Review `scoop status`, buckets, app versions and rollback options first.

commands.title: Reinstall a broken Scoop-managed application
commands.summary: Reinstall one identified Scoop app using Scoop's own commands after checking its manifest and persisted data.
commands.code:
scoop info app-name
scoop reinstall app-name
commands.safety: Replace app-name with the exact app. Reinstall can alter the current version and links; back up app-specific configuration and review Scoop's persisted directory first.

commands.title: Uninstall one Scoop-managed application
commands.summary: Remove one application managed by Scoop.
commands.safety: Replace with exact app name. Review persisted data and whether other tools depend on the app before removal.

commands.title: Inspect UniGetUI package-manager health
commands.summary: Open UniGetUI manager health page to inspect package-manager failures and available repair actions.
commands.safety: Requires UniGetUI CLI installed and available on PATH. Opens UI; no repair is run by this command.

commands.title: List updates from a selected UniGetUI manager
commands.summary: Query available package updates through UniGetUI's CLI for a specified package manager.
commands.safety: Requires supported UniGetUI version and selected manager. Replace winget with a manager ID actually enabled on this system. The output is manager-scoped, not a complete OS patch report.

commands.title: Update packages through UniGetUI
commands.summary: Queue package updates through UniGetUI for supported managers.
commands.safety: Requires UniGetUI CLI and a configured session. Changes installed packages. Review manager health, ignored updates, package IDs and maintenance window first. The command returns failure if operations fail or time out.

commands.title: Repair one package through UniGetUI
commands.summary: Use UniGetUI's package repair flow, which uninstalls and reinstalls the selected package.
commands.code: uniget.exe package repair --manager winget --id Publisher.Package --remove-data false --interactive true --wait true
commands.safety: Replace with the exact manager ID and package ID. This uninstalls then reinstalls; `--remove-data false` does not guarantee vendor app data is preserved. Back up app-specific data and confirm package identity first.

commands.title: Uninstall one package through UniGetUI
commands.summary: Uninstall one package with manager and package identity specified.
commands.code: uniget.exe package uninstall --manager winget --id Publisher.Package --remove-data false --interactive true --wait true
commands.safety: Replace exact manager and package IDs. Review scope and app data before proceeding. Do not set remove-data true unless the user explicitly wants data removed.

commands.title: Repair WinGet manager health through UniGetUI
commands.summary: Run UniGetUI's documented WinGet manager repair action when Manager Health reports WinGet malfunctioning.
commands.safety: Requires the current UniGetUI CLI and elevated privileges. This action can clear WinGet temp files, reset sources and repair App Installer; record custom sources first. Confirm the CLI syntax for the installed release.

commands.title: Audit supported applications with Ninite Pro Classic
commands.summary: Generate an audit report showing Ninite-supported application versions and update availability.
commands.safety: Requires Ninite Pro Classic license and its executable. Newer Pro web interface differs; use its inline docs. Audit only covers Ninite-supported applications, not all installed software.

commands.title: Update supported apps with Ninite Pro Classic
commands.summary: Update only supported apps that are outdated, without installing missing selections.
commands.safety: Commercial license required. This is a silent system-changing operation. Check supported apps, exclusions and report path. Pro Classic only; newer web interface may differ.

commands.title: Force reinstallation of a supported Ninite app
commands.summary: Use Ninite Pro Classic /repair for an identified supported application when a repair/reinstall is needed.
commands.safety: Requires Pro Classic. Replace Firefox with a supported exact app selection. Reinstalling can change app version/configuration; verify current app list and preserve profile data. Not available as a generic repair for arbitrary software.

commands.title: Open Windows Installer and WinGet logs
commands.summary: Open the relevant logs and inspect the exact failure before attempting repair or uninstall.
commands.safety: Read-only except opening tools. WinGet logs exist only for WinGet operations. Sanitize paths and account names before sharing logs.

commands.title: Re-register Microsoft Store for the current user
commands.summary: Re-register Store package manifest for current user if Store itself is damaged and the package exists.
commands.code:
Get-AppxPackage -Name Microsoft.WindowsStore | Select-Object Name,PackageFullName,InstallLocation
Get-AppxPackage -Name Microsoft.WindowsStore | ForEach-Object { Add-AppxPackage -DisableDevelopmentMode -Register (Join-Path $_.InstallLocation 'AppxManifest.xml') }
commands.safety: Changes current-user app package registration. Run only if the package exists and Store-specific repair is indicated. Do not bulk re-register every AppX package or run this on managed multi-user systems without testing.

commands.title: Export WinGet package inventory for a maintenance record
commands.summary: Export a package inventory file for review and later comparison.
commands.safety: Creates a local inventory file. Export does not include every installed application or necessarily every installer source. Review and sanitize before attaching to a ticket.

commands.title: Check for pending restart indicators
commands.summary: Check common Windows servicing and update reboot markers before starting another maintenance run.
commands.safety: Read-only indicators only. Do not force a reboot based on registry markers alone; confirm user work, BitLocker recovery access, backup and service/installer activity.

commands.title: List Debian/Ubuntu package updates
commands.summary: Refresh package metadata and list upgradable packages.
commands.safety: Refreshes package metadata and displays candidates; does not install package upgrades. Confirm repositories and held packages.

commands.title: Upgrade Debian/Ubuntu packages
commands.summary: Apply available package upgrades after reviewing the package list.
commands.code:
sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade
commands.safety: Changes installed packages. Review removals and dependency changes before confirming; avoid `full-upgrade` on production systems without a planned change and recovery route.

commands.title: Check Fedora/RHEL package updates
commands.summary: Check available updates without applying them.
commands.safety: Returns update availability; exit code 100 can indicate updates are available and is not necessarily an error.

commands.title: Upgrade Fedora/RHEL packages
commands.summary: Apply package updates after reviewing repository and package changes.
commands.safety: Changes installed packages. Review transaction summary, kernel changes and service restart/reboot requirements before confirming.

commands.title: Check Arch Linux package updates
commands.summary: Refresh package database and inspect pending updates using the package manager's supported query path.
commands.safety: Requires the checkupdates helper from pacman-contrib on many systems. Do not partially upgrade Arch systems; read the news and follow full-upgrade guidance.

commands.title: Perform a full Arch Linux upgrade
commands.summary: Synchronize repositories and perform the supported full system upgrade.
commands.safety: Changes the entire installed system. Arch does not support partial upgrades; read Arch news first and avoid interrupting package transactions.

commands.title: Uninstall a supported application with Ninite Pro Classic
commands.summary: Uninstall one selected Ninite-supported application through the Pro Classic command-line interface.
commands.safety: Requires a valid Ninite Pro Classic license. Replace Firefox with a supported exact app selection. This changes the endpoint and may remove app data; preserve browser profiles and user data first. Newer Pro web interface has different controls.

workflows.title: Safe update session
workflows.description: Inventory the machine, preview each configured app manager, check OS servicing separately, then apply only approved updates.
workflows.sequence: Identify package managers first. Run only the matching manager's preview. Compare duplicate package ownership before updating. Record exclusions and pins. Schedule installation and reboot separately.
workflows.warning: The commands do not provide one universal all-app inventory. A package can appear in more than one manager; avoid double updates. OS, Store, firmware and drivers are separate channels.

workflows.title: Recover a stuck or failed Windows Update
workflows.description: Capture error codes and logs, run the supported troubleshooter, repair system files and only then reset update caches if evidence supports it.
workflows.sequence: Preserve the error code and logs first. Check free space and services. Run Get Help troubleshooter. If corruption is indicated, use DISM then SFC. Use reversible cache rename only after earlier steps fail. Re-run update check and verify history.
workflows.warning: Cache reset changes state and re-downloads updates. Do not delete cache folders blindly or reset components while servicing is active.

workflows.title: Repair a broken application
workflows.description: Identify the exact package manager and package identity, collect logs, try native repair, then reinstall or uninstall only when appropriate.
workflows.sequence: Find exact app, manager, source, version and scope. Preserve app data/config. Use native repair if supported. If repair unavailable, back up app data then use manager-specific reinstall. Uninstall only after user approval and data-retention check. Verify launch and version.
workflows.warning: Repair may reinstall or uninstall/reinstall. Never assume user data survives. Do not use generic registry cleaners or guessed MSI product codes.

workflows.title: Repair a broken package manager
workflows.description: Inspect the package manager's own logs and health, repair the manager itself, then re-audit package state.
workflows.sequence: Capture manager version and sources. Check the manager's own health and logs. Apply only the matching documented repair. Preserve custom sources and configuration. Re-run installed/update listings and confirm no package ownership was lost.
workflows.warning: Manager repair can reset sources or remove caches. Export custom configuration before changing it.

workflows.title: Uninstall a stuck or damaged application
workflows.description: Inspect installed-app registration and identify the correct manager before using the supported uninstall path.
workflows.sequence: Confirm app identity, publisher, uninstall scope and data-retention preference. Use the manager that owns the package. If manager metadata is missing, use the vendor's official uninstaller or Windows Apps UI. Inspect MSI logs for MSI failures.
workflows.warning: Do not delete Program Files folders, registry uninstall keys or Windows Installer cache as a substitute for uninstall. Shared dependencies and user data may be affected.

workflows.title: Recover from a half-finished application update
workflows.description: Determine whether the installer is still active, waiting for reboot, or failed; avoid starting a second installer over the first.
workflows.sequence: Check active installer and servicing activity. Capture the original error/log. Confirm pending restart state. If the installer is still active, do not terminate it. If it exited with failure, use vendor repair or manager repair for the exact package. Verify version, app launch and event logs.
workflows.warning: Do not kill msiexec or Windows servicing processes as a quick fix. Do not start overlapping installs or force a rollback while an installer transaction is active.

principles: No automatic background polling; inventory occurs only on technician request or explicit scheduled task.
Detect manager ownership before updating to avoid duplicate package updates.
Application updates, Windows Update, Microsoft Store, firmware and drivers remain separate channels.
Preview before bulk changes; preserve package pins, exclusions and source identity.
Never terminate active Windows Installer or servicing processes as a generic recovery action.
Back up user data and application configuration before repair/reinstall/uninstall when the vendor may remove it.
Prefer native repair; then controlled reinstall; uninstall only with explicit approval.
Every operation must record manager, package ID, version, source, scope, exit code, logs, start/end time and verification.
Do not claim a live update status from a static website. Live inventory requires a local INTA agent or supported manager integration.
Copy controls never execute commands; a future local runner must show exact plan and request explicit confirmation.
